value.overview: The Collared Redstart, also called the Collared Whitestart, is a small, lively New World warbler of the Central American highlands. It is endemic to the mountains of Costa Rica and western-central Panama, where it occupies cool, humid forests and nearby edges. Its bright yellow face and underparts contrast with a dark hood and collar, while its energetic movements and frequently fanned tail make it one of the more conspicuous small birds in montane forests.
value.classification: The Collared Redstart belongs to the New World warbler family Parulidae and the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Myioborus torquatus, and it is generally treated as a monotypic species without recognized subspecies.
value.identification: This small warbler has a bright yellow face, throat, and underparts, a grayish back, and a dark head and breast forming a distinctive collar-like pattern. The crown is typically orange or chestnut, and the tail is dark with conspicuous pale or white outer feathers. It is active and often shows its tail while moving through vegetation. Its bold facial pattern and dark collar help separate it from other Myioborus warblers in Costa Rica.
value.rangeHabitat: The Collared Redstart has a restricted range in the highlands of Costa Rica and western-central Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly along the Cordillera de Talamanca and other major mountain ranges, including highland forest areas such as Monteverde, Poás, and the mountains around San Gerardo de Dota. It uses humid montane and cloud forests, forest borders, dense second growth, bamboo thickets, and other shrubby vegetation, generally at middle to high elevations, often roughly 1,200–3,000 meters.
value.migrationStatus: It is primarily resident in Costa Rica and does not undertake long-distance migration. Individuals may make local or seasonal movements along mountain slopes, including limited shifts in elevation in response to breeding conditions, weather, or food availability.
value.breeding: The species breeds in the montane highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. Breeding activity in Costa Rica is associated largely with the rainy season, when insect food is abundant, although timing can vary with elevation and local conditions. Pairs usually place a small cup-shaped nest in dense vegetation near or on the ground, where surrounding foliage provides concealment. The female generally performs much of the incubation, while both adults participate in territorial defense and care of young.
value.dietFeeding: The Collared Redstart feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods collected from leaves, branches, moss, and dense understory vegetation. It may also take small fruits or other soft plant foods when available. While foraging, it moves rapidly through shrubs and lower forest layers, frequently flicking or fanning its tail. These sudden movements may flush hidden insects and make them easier to capture.
value.behavior: This is an active, restless bird that commonly forages alone, in pairs, or with mixed-species feeding groups. It frequently hops through dense vegetation and pauses briefly before making short sallies after prey. Tail spreading is a characteristic behavior. The species is usually easiest to detect by its bright plumage, energetic movements, and sharp calls in cool, humid mountain forests, especially along trails, forest edges, and natural openings.

conservation.populationTrend: The species is not generally recognized as undergoing a major global decline, although its restricted highland range means that local populations could be affected by habitat changes.
